progression.startsWith: Five bottles on the prep room bench have lost their labels. The list says they hold cyclohexane, cyclohexene, ethanol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol and ethanoic acid. They're all colourless liquids, so looking won't help. You can't see a double bond or an O H group, but you can see what it does. Three quick tests, each watching for one group, can rule candidates out.
progression.stopsAfter: predicting the reagent and the positive and negative observations for each group; reading green and orange dichromate results with their limits; explaining fresh portions and the order; reporting each group separately; excluding candidates from a list; stating what the three tests cannot show.

teaching.task: Five colourless liquids have lost their labels, and you know which five compounds they are. How can three quick tests, each watching for one group, tell you which bottle is which?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) you can't see a group, but you can see what it does; three tests, each watching for one group, rule candidates out (1); (2) pick a reaction only one group does fast, with a visible change: predict before testing (2); (3) bromine adds across a C=C and is used up, so the orange fades; an alkane has no C=C to open; bright light lets an alkane substitute slowly, so test in room light and read at once (3); (4) a carboxylic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, so it protonates hydrogen carbonate; carbonic acid breaks up into water and CO₂, so it fizzes; CO₂ turns limewater milky; an alcohol is far too weak (4); (5) a primary or secondary alcohol is oxidised and orange dichromate is reduced to green Cr³⁺; a tertiary alcohol has no H on its C–OH carbon, so it stays orange (5); (6) green means something was oxidised, and aldehydes do it too; orange means no primary or secondary alcohol detected, not no OH (6); (7) fresh portions make the tests independent, so the order sets the hazard: mildest first, Cr(VI) last as a demonstration (7); (8) one molecule can carry two groups, so a "yes" does not mean "no" for the others: run all three and report each (8); (9) the worked exclusion, where the "no" results do half the work (9); (10) the limits: two candidates can give identical results; primary against secondary; position; groups, not structure (10); memory aid (11); attempts (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Five bottles on the prep room bench have lost their labels. Each test borrows a reaction from Module 7. First, the carbon to carbon double bond. Next, the carboxylic acid. Then the hydroxyl group. Green tells you something in the tube was oxidised. Use a fresh portion of the sample for each test, so one reagent can't spoil the next result. Here's the trap. Back to the bench. Suppose another bottle had given no change in all three tests. One line for the three tests: fizz, fade, green. Your turn. No fizz rules out hexanoic acid. Last one. The conclusion isn't supported. So, when you meet an unknown, ask three questions.
teaching.openingDecision: Five bottles on the prep room bench have lost their labels. The list says they hold cyclohexane, cyclohexene, ethanol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol and ethanoic acid. They're all colourless liquids, so looking won't help. You can't see a double bond or an O H group, but you can see what it does. Three quick tests, each watching for one group, can rule candidates out.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "An unknown liquid is one of these four compounds: hexane, hexan-1-ol, hex-5-en-1-ol, hexanoic acid. Separate portions of the liquid were tested. Solid sodium hydrogen carbonate: no effervescence. Bromine water, in normal room light: orange to colourless within seconds. Acidified potassium dichromate, warmed: orange to green. Identify the unknown, and justify your answer with reference to each result." Answer: hex-5-en-1-ol. No fizz rules out hexanoic acid; the fade supports a C=C, ruling out hexane and hexan-1-ol; only hex-5-en-1-ol remains, and the green is consistent with its OH group (not the deciding result). Crossed mistake: "hexan-1-ol: it turned dichromate green" (using one result and ignoring another; pack trap "one test treated as full structure"). Revision 2: hexane replaces hex-1-ene (author note c fallback), so the identification no longer depends on an alkene staying orange. (A2) "Liquid Q is known to be an alkane, an alkene, an alcohol or a carboxylic acid; no other reactive groups are present. Q produced no effervescence when solid sodium hydrogen carbonate was added. A student concluded that Q is an alcohol. Evaluate the student's conclusion. Outline TWO further tests, with expected results, stating what each result would support, and one limit of these tests." Answer: not supported; no fizz rules out only a carboxylic acid, so Q could be an alkane, an alkene or an alcohol; fresh portion with bromine water (fades within seconds: C=C supported); fresh portion warmed with acidified dichromate (if the bromine stayed orange, green supports a primary or secondary alcohol); limit: orange leaves an alkane or a tertiary alcohol, which these tests can't separate. Crossed mistake: "no fizz, so Q is an alcohol" (treating one "no" as a "yes" for something else; site Think First idea, original wording; pack trap "alcohol OH assumed acidic enough for carbonate", turned round).
teaching.curriculumScope:
Syllabus dotpoint (as printed; NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p58; C8-IQ2-01 is this project's local catalogue ID, not a code printed in the syllabus), quoted from ../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y12.json:

"conduct qualitative investigations to test for the presence in organic molecules of the following functional groups:
- carbon–carbon double bonds
- hydroxyl groups
- carboxylic acids (ACSCH130)"

(The dash in "carbon–carbon" is an en dash as printed, not an em dash.) This video teaches the tests and the reasoning; the investigation (controls, method, risk) is chem-m8-p05.

design.visualSystem: test tubes, racks, bottles and limewater as painted plates listed by filename, never stretched, never cross-faded between different rack sets; no people, hands or faces (drops, shaking and the bung are coded motion); molecules coded in the c08a style; the decision flowchart and the candidate strip coded (abstract diagrams); at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; one test on screen at a time until the flowchart; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (answer, key reason, one crossed mistake, about 15 to 30 s); original HSC-style questions only; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims ("usually", "points to", "supports", "detected").
